sentences.text: Programming Fundamentals: Procedural programming develops step-by-step solutions using variables, decisions, repetition and functions, with attention to tracing and debugging small programs.
Object-Oriented Programming: Object-based software design organizes state and behaviour into classes, exploring encapsulation, inheritance and reusable abstractions for structured applications.
Discrete Mathematics: Mathematical structures for computing connect logic, sets, relations and graph reasoning to precise statements about finite computational problems.
Data Structures: Organizing collections through lists, stacks, queues, trees and related structures supports efficient storage, access and modification of program data.
Database Management Systems: Relational data organization uses schemas, structured queries and integrity constraints to store linked records and maintain consistent information during updates.
Probability and Statistics: Mathematical treatment of uncertainty combines probability distributions, summary statistics and inference to interpret variable observations and reason about evidence.
Design and Analysis of Algorithms: Systematic algorithm design compares strategies for solving computational problems and evaluates their resource costs as input sizes change.
Operating Systems: System software coordinates processes, memory and shared resources so concurrent programs can run safely while using underlying computing hardware.
Computer Networks: Protocols and layered architectures that enable digital devices to exchange data over connected systems.
Software Engineering: Disciplined software development connects requirements, design, testing and maintenance to the construction of dependable applications by collaborating teams.

Linear Algebra for Computing: Vector spaces, matrices and linear transformations provide mathematical tools for representing numerical observations and reasoning about computations in multiple dimensions.
Artificial Intelligence: Intelligent problem solving examines search, knowledge representation and reasoning methods for choosing actions under specified goals and constraints.
Machine Learning: Data-driven methods that learn patterns from examples to make predictions on unseen observations.
Data Engineering: Data preparation workflows organize, clean and transform collections into dependable inputs for downstream analytical systems, emphasizing consistency across processing stages.
Compiler Design: Translation of programming languages connects lexical analysis, syntax and semantic checking to the construction of representations suitable for execution.
Information Retrieval: Retrieval of relevant items from document collections examines representations, ranking and evaluation, linking information needs with indexed textual evidence.
Natural Language Processing: Computational methods for processing, understanding and generating human language through symbolic, statistical and contextual representations.
Deep Learning: Multilayer neural methods for learning hierarchical representations from data, building on Machine Learning.
Computer Vision: Visual pattern interpretation applies learned representations to images, considering recognition tasks and evaluation of predictions from visual observations.
Distributed Systems: Cooperating processes across multiple machines coordinate computation while reasoning about communication, consistency and failures in shared systems.
These regulations describe the synthetic B.Tech Computer Science and Engineering program for academic year 2026-2027 in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering.
The institution is situated in the invented teaching location of Velmora, Teralin Learning District.
Its degree duration is 4 years across 8 semesters.
The compact curriculum is an educational design and does not claim accreditation or equivalence to a real institution's regulations.
The curriculum identifies courses by stable codes rather than informal nicknames.
A course's semester indicates its normal place in the program.
Credits express its contribution to the academic record; marks express performance in an assessment.
A laboratory is a separate course with its own code and credits, even when it is closely connected to a theory subject.
Listed electives are the fixed choices of this synthetic cohort, not a menu of additional unlisted subjects.
Students should consult the semester course structure alongside the prerequisite register when preparing their study plan.
Prerequisites describe earlier courses that supply necessary foundations.
Corequisites identify theory subjects studied in the same semester as their associated laboratories.
Treating a corequisite as an earlier prerequisite would misrepresent the intended sequence.
The register supplies the complete declared relationships; an omitted relationship must not be invented from a similarity between course names.
Different cohorts attend odd semesters together and even semesters together.
The academic calendar therefore contains two terms within one academic year, rather than eight consecutive teaching periods.
It specifies registration milestones and examination windows.
Only the NLP course has a separately fixed examination date.
Dates for other individual courses, or future reassessments, should not be inferred from the first day of an examination window.
The minimum attendance is 75% in each enrolled course.
It applies to theory, laboratories, projects and seminars separately.
Attendance is the proportion of held scheduled sessions that the student attended, evaluated without rounding the percentage upward.
A strong attendance record in one course does not cancel a shortage in another.
Students with insufficient participation are ineligible for the affected course's end-semester evaluation.
There is no condonation route in this synthetic policy.
Approved leave does not automatically count as classroom participation.
A verified recording error may be corrected because it changes the underlying record, not the required threshold.
A shortage requires re-enrollment at the next offering.
Internal assessment marks cannot waive attendance eligibility, and completed laboratory records do not create an exception to the general rule.
The course has 100 total marks: 40 internal assessment marks and 60 end-semester marks.
Passing requires at least 50 total marks and at least 24 end-semester marks.
Both conditions apply together; there is no separate internal minimum.
Attendance eligibility remains a separate requirement.
Internal assessment consists of a 20-mark midterm assessment and 20 marks of continuous coursework.
Written examinations support theory courses, while practical demonstrations and viva support laboratory assessment.
Projects and seminars use progress review, portfolio work and a final demonstration or viva.
These different modes use the same numerical scheme; they do not introduce alternative passing totals.
An eligible student who fails either pass condition may take reassessment at the next announced opportunity.
The present calendar does not specify that date.

Attendance ineligibility is a different situation from an eligible student's unsuccessful examination performance, and its recovery rule is re-enrollment rather than an assumed reassessment entitlement.
Absolute grade bands are applied only after the pass requirements are satisfied.
Recorded final marks are whole numbers.
An F grade carries zero grade points.
Attendance ineligibility is recorded as NE and withholds the semester GPA until the course is completed.
The GPA is a credit-weighted mean; credits and grade points therefore have distinct roles.
For a detailed participation decision, consult the Attendance Policy.
For grade bands and assessment conditions, consult Examination Regulations.
For experiment records and demonstrations, use Laboratory Guidelines.
The calendar supplies dates, while syllabi supply course content.
Together these documents describe one academic world without making every document reproduce every rule in full.
B.Tech Computer Science and Engineering (B.Tech CSE) spans four years and eight semesters in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering.
The curriculum below contains 47 courses totaling 160 credits.
It describes the fixed synthetic cohort for 2026-2027; it is not a real accreditation document.
Theory subjects, laboratories, seminars, projects and fixed electives have distinct roles but contribute to the same program.
The first semester develops programming, mathematical and digital foundations alongside communication and design practice.
Its studio introduces the habit of explaining a technical artifact, while the laboratory connects program tracing with actual execution.
The second semester extends programming into object-based organization and adds discrete mathematical reasoning, computer organization and further mathematics.
The technical communication seminar accompanies this shift from individual exercises toward explaining structured technical work.
The third semester develops data organization, relational information and the mathematical treatment of uncertainty.
Data Structures and Database Management Systems each have a distinct laboratory for practical exploration.
The fourth semester turns toward computing systems and collaborative development.
Operating Systems and Computer Networks examine different layers of execution and communication.
Software Engineering connects program design with development practices, while Linear Algebra for Computing prepares later numerical representations.
The fifth semester establishes the main AI pathway.
Artificial Intelligence emphasizes intelligent problem solving, while Machine Learning introduces prediction from examples.
Data Engineering and Theory of Computation provide contrasting perspectives.
A software project and the ML laboratory connect these themes with artifacts and observations.
The sixth semester brings language-centered applications into focus.
NLP uses earlier AI and ML foundations; Information Retrieval supplies a related view of relevance and ranking.
Compiler Design, Responsible Computing and the research seminar broaden the context in which language and data systems are studied.
The seventh semester develops multilayer neural methods and visual interpretation while retaining systems and security perspectives.
Deep Learning has its own laboratory.
Capstone Project I follows the earlier software project and research seminar rather than replacing their preparatory roles.
The final semester contains Applied AI Systems and Cloud Computing Fundamentals as the cohort's fixed electives.
Professional Practice and Industry Practice Project accompany Capstone Project II.
Project II depends on Project I, preserving the declared two-stage capstone relationship.

Computational methods for processing, understanding and generating human language through symbolic, statistical and contextual representations.
Earlier-course prerequisites: Artificial Intelligence (HCE-CSE501); Machine Learning (HCE-CSE502).
The related course is Natural Language Processing Laboratory (HCE-CSE605), a 2-credit laboratory in Semester 6.
The theory course is its same-semester corequisite, not an earlier prerequisite.
The laboratory's own earlier prerequisites are Artificial Intelligence (HCE-CSE501); Machine Learning (HCE-CSE502).
Prepare text and explain representation choices.
Construct count-based and weighted language representations.
Explain sequence context, attention and Transformer representations.
Evaluate semantic similarity and retrieval experiments.
Topics: Text normalization; Stop words; Stemming and lemmatization; Text Preprocessing; Tokenization.
Text preparation begins with the decisions that turn a raw string into a usable sequence.
Students consider capitalization, punctuation and spacing alongside text normalization.
Tokenization establishes the units that later representations count or encode.
Stop words, stemming and lemmatization are examined as choices with consequences rather than operations that should be applied automatically.
An abbreviated course notice and a complete sentence can lose different information when cleaned in the same way.
The unit connects visible changes in the text to the task being attempted.
Topics: Vocabulary; One-hot encoding; Term and document frequency; Bag of Words; N-Grams; TF-IDF; Cosine Similarity.
A vocabulary supplies a shared coordinate system for a collection.
One-hot encoding identifies individual terms; Bag of Words counts their occurrences while setting aside order.
N-Grams retain short sequences and therefore preserve some local context.
Term frequency and document frequency support TF-IDF, where frequent words within one document are interpreted alongside their prevalence across the collection.
Cosine Similarity compares vector direction rather than simply rewarding a long document.
Students discuss what a count-based representation can capture and what it loses when two passages use different words for related ideas.
Topics: Embedding geometry; Distributional context; Word vector evaluation; Word Embeddings; Word2Vec; CBOW; Skip-Gram.
Distributed word representations place vocabulary items in a dense numerical space rather than allocating an independent coordinate to every word.
The unit connects Word Embeddings with patterns of distributional context.
Word2Vec is considered through its two training directions: CBOW uses surrounding context to predict a target, while Skip-Gram starts with a target to predict nearby words.
Vector geometry supports comparisons among learned words, but closeness does not automatically prove synonymy.
Evaluation asks whether a representation captures useful relationships for a particular language task and where a single representation per word misses contextual variation.

Topics: Sequence context; Recurrent model intuition; Contextual representations; Masked language modeling; Autoregressive / next-token language modeling; GPT; Language Models; Attention; Transformers; BERT.
Sequence models introduce the importance of surrounding tokens and their order.
Recurrent model intuition provides a point of comparison for contextual representations.
Attention assigns differing relevance to parts of a sequence when constructing a representation; Transformers organize these operations into an architecture that can relate distant positions.
BERT introduces an encoder-oriented contextual representation and masked language modeling.
GPT provides the contrasting decoder-oriented, autoregressive / next-token language modeling approach used for text generation: successive tokens are predicted from preceding context.
The unit distinguishes an architecture from a training objective and a pretrained model family.
Language Models connect token prediction with the use of context, without assuming that fluent text guarantees factual correctness.
Topics: Sentence representations; Retrieval evaluation; Limitations of similarity measures; Semantic Similarity; Semantic Search.
Sentence representations extend the discussion from isolated vocabulary items to complete pieces of text.
Semantic Similarity asks how closely two statements relate in meaning, while Semantic Search uses such representations to retrieve relevant evidence from a collection.
Students connect similarity measures with retrieval evaluation and inspect ambiguous matches rather than treating a high score as a complete explanation.
A query may use terminology absent from a relevant passage.
Conversely, overlapping words may refer to different academic topics.
The unit emphasizes identifying evidence, explaining ranking behaviour and stating the limitations of the chosen representation.

Students should be able to explain how a representation changes the information available to a language task, compare count-based and distributed approaches, and interpret semantic retrieval evidence with appropriate limitations.
The course connects Machine Learning methods with language applications.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a subsequent workshop application, not a sixth formal syllabus unit.
Internal assessment contains a 20-mark midterm and 20 marks of continuous coursework.
Written end-semester assessment is used for this theory course.
The associated laboratory uses the same marking scheme with practical demonstration and viva.

Data-driven methods that learn patterns from examples to make predictions on unseen observations.
Earlier-course prerequisites: Probability and Statistics (HCE-CSE303); Design and Analysis of Algorithms (HCE-CSE304); Linear Algebra for Computing (HCE-CSE404).
The related course is Machine Learning Laboratory (HCE-CSE505), a 2-credit laboratory in Semester 5.
The laboratory's own earlier prerequisites are Probability and Statistics (HCE-CSE303); Linear Algebra for Computing (HCE-CSE404).
Train and evaluate predictive models with suitable metrics.
Explain feature preparation and model validation.
Topics: Learning paradigms; Features and labels; Training and test partitions.
Learning foundations distinguish supervised tasks with labels from unsupervised exploration of structure.
Features describe observations, while labels specify the target when one is available.
Training and test partitions separate model construction from later evaluation.
The unit makes clear that success on examples used during learning is not sufficient evidence of generalization.
Students describe the prediction problem before deciding whether a model family is appropriate.
Topics: Linear regression; Logistic regression; Decision trees; Nearest neighbours.
Supervised prediction connects linear regression with numerical targets and logistic regression with class decisions.
Decision trees and nearest neighbours offer contrasting ways to organize predictions.
The emphasis is on what information a model uses and how its assumptions affect outputs.
Classification and regression share the use of examples but produce different kinds of decisions.
Feature preparation is interpreted in relation to the task, not treated as an unrelated preprocessing ritual.
Topics: Cross-validation; Classification metrics; Bias and variance; Regularization.
Evaluation and generalization use cross-validation and classification metrics to inspect performance beyond a single score.
Bias and variance provide a vocabulary for discussing underfitting and overfitting, while regularization controls excessive adaptation to particular training observations.
Data leakage is examined as a failure of experimental design rather than a mysterious property of the model.
Students compare the evidence supporting a result with the conclusion being claimed.
Topics: Clustering; Principal component analysis; Distance measures.
Unsupervised learning considers clustering and principal component analysis as different ways to explore observations without supplied prediction labels.
Distance measures influence which samples appear related.
Clusters summarize patterns in a chosen representation; they are not automatically meaningful categories.
Dimensionality reduction changes the coordinate view and may preserve some relationships more clearly than others.
Interpretation should therefore connect the numerical result with the question that motivated the analysis.
Topics: Perceptron; Gradient descent; Basic multilayer networks; Responsible model use.
The neural learning introduction uses the perceptron and basic multilayer networks to connect predictions with adjustable parameters.
Gradient descent supplies the idea of incremental improvement through an objective.
The treatment prepares students for later Deep Learning without making this course a complete study of large neural architectures.
Responsible model use includes explaining limitations and examining whether evaluation justifies applying a model to observations unlike those used for training.

Students should be able to describe a learning task, select an appropriate evaluation approach, distinguish feature preparation from model fitting, and recognize unsupported claims caused by overfitting or leakage.
NLP later applies predictive and representational ideas to language.
Deep Learning develops multilayer neural methods more extensively.
Those connections do not make the three courses interchangeable.
Multilayer neural methods for learning hierarchical representations from data, building on Machine Learning.
Earlier-course prerequisites: Machine Learning (HCE-CSE502); Linear Algebra for Computing (HCE-CSE404).
The related course is Deep Learning Laboratory (HCE-CSE705), a 2-credit laboratory in Semester 7.
The laboratory's own earlier prerequisites are Machine Learning (HCE-CSE502); Linear Algebra for Computing (HCE-CSE404).
Train neural networks and diagnose generalization issues.
Compare convolutional, recurrent and attention-based architectures.
Multilayer perceptrons compose successive transformations into representations used for prediction.
Forward propagation describes the flow from inputs to outputs, while backpropagation relates an objective to changes in parameters.
The discussion distinguishes model structure from the procedure used to fit it.
Machine Learning supplies the earlier concepts of examples, generalization and evaluation; Linear Algebra for Computing supplies the vector and matrix language used to describe transformations.
Optimization concerns how parameters are adjusted during learning.
Regularization addresses excessive adaptation to the available observations.
A small training error can coexist with poor behaviour on new data, so the course examines model evaluation alongside the training process.
Students explain learning choices and their consequences rather than interpreting every change in a loss curve as evidence of a better deployed model.
The emphasis remains on the approved major topics, without adding a separate institutional benchmark requirement.
Convolutional neural networks organize computations around local patterns and shared transformations.
This offers a useful connection to Computer Vision, another Semester 7 course, while the two subjects retain different focuses.
Deep Learning examines the neural architecture and representation-learning perspective; Computer Vision concerns visual interpretation tasks.
Comparisons should account for the kind of input and evaluation problem rather than assuming that every neural network architecture suits every observation.
Recurrent networks provide a way to carry information along a sequence.
Attention-based architectures offer another view of relationships between positions.
These themes connect with the contextual language representations encountered in NLP during Semester 6.
NLP is not declared as a prerequisite for this course; its appearance earlier in the curriculum is a conceptual connection, not an extra registration rule.
The comparison helps students explain why the same family of methods can appear in different application-oriented subjects.
Model evaluation examines the evidence supporting a neural system's predictions.
Students distinguish successful learning on a particular collection from a claim of universal understanding.
Representations are interpreted through the task and data used to construct them.
The associated laboratory provides a setting for observing trained behaviour and explaining an artifact during practical assessment.
No named model, computing platform or commercial service is mandated by this synthetic syllabus.

Students should be able to explain forward and backward propagation, connect optimization with model fitting, discuss regularization and generalization, and compare convolutional, recurrent and attention-based architectures.
The topic headings above organize the approved major topics for reading; they are not a newly defined five-unit contract.
Deep Learning shares predictive evaluation with Machine Learning and contextual representation ideas with NLP, while concentrating on multilayer neural methods.

Students must maintain at least 75% attendance in each enrolled course.
The requirement applies separately to theory courses, laboratories, projects and seminars.
Classroom participation in one subject cannot be transferred to another subject's attendance record.
There is one institutional threshold; laboratory participation does not use an additional or reduced percentage.
Attendance eligibility refers to participation in scheduled sessions that were actually held.
It is not a score on an assignment and it is not the total number of credits registered.
When discussing a shortage, identify the affected course and the underlying session record.
A general statement that a student attends college regularly is insufficient to establish eligibility in every subject.
The attendance percentage is the number of attended scheduled sessions divided by the number of held scheduled sessions, multiplied by 100.
Compare the unrounded result with the minimum.
Rounding a lower value upward for display does not make it eligible.
The relevant denominator is held sessions, not all dates printed in a calendar or an assumed total from a different course.
For an illustrative arithmetic example, attending 15 of 20 held sessions gives 75% and reaches the threshold.
Attending 14 of those same 20 sessions does not.
These counts explain the rule; they are not a mandated number of sessions for a semester.
Course timetables and total session counts are not specified in the fact contract.
A percentage below the minimum is an attendance shortage.
The student is ineligible for that course's end-semester evaluation.
This includes a written examination, laboratory practical, project demonstration or seminar evaluation according to the course's delivery mode.
Good performance in continuous coursework does not cancel a shortage.
Internal marks alone cannot waive the participation requirement.
Reaching the attendance minimum permits end-semester evaluation under the policy; it does not establish that a student will meet the examination pass conditions.
Conversely, an estimated high examination score does not establish eligibility before the participation rule is satisfied.
Examination Regulations explain the marks needed to pass after eligibility is established.
No condonation is available in this synthetic policy.
Approved leave does not automatically count as an attended session.

These guidelines describe the common record and demonstration requirements; they do not prescribe a numbered experiment list or silently introduce tools and downloads that the workshop has not yet implemented.
Submit a dated record for each assigned experiment, including inputs, method, observations and conclusion, by the term's records milestone.
The record connects a result with the input and method that produced it.
An observation may be surprising or incomplete; explain it rather than replacing it with an unsupported expected answer.
A conclusion should state what the particular experiment supports, without claiming that one successful example establishes universal performance.
The calendar's term milestone supplies the due date, so this document does not invent a separate submission date.
Complete every assigned experiment before the end-semester practical; the experiment list will be defined in later laboratory documents.
Demonstrate working results and explain the method during the practical viva; project labs also demonstrate their final artifact.
The demonstration asks the student to connect an artifact with its procedure and results.
A record provides evidence of practical work, while the viva provides an opportunity to explain choices and limitations.
